# Microorganisms in household products

## 1. Introduction
Opening frame for **Microorganisms in household products** — what the topic is, why it matters, a real-world hook (Nepal where possible), the map of what follows, and the learning outcomes (biology-plan.md §3.1, block I). Prose depth is written in the Microbes in Human Welfare fill pass.

## 2. Hierarchy body — every syllabus sub-point
### Microorganisms in household products

Fill order per concept: definition → structure → process → significance (§3.2). Step-by-step numbered points, Pioneer style.

Fermentation is household chemistry. *Lactobacillus* turns milk into curd; yeast raises dough and ferments drinks; bacteria and fungi ripen cheese. Every one of these is a microbe digesting sugar and, as a by-product, changing the food — adding flavour, texture, preservation, and in the case of curd, nutrition (vitamin B12).

## 3. Classified tables

Tables carry examples in every classification and characteristics row, ≤ 12 rows, and each is referenced from the body text (§3.3).

**Concept flow — one principle behind every household fermentation (study in this order)**

| Step | Principle | Example |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Microbes are grown on a sugar-rich food | Milk lactose, flour starch, fruit juice |
| 2 | They metabolise it anaerobically (or semi-anaerobically) | Yeast respires without oxygen |
| 3 | The products are acids, alcohol and CO2 | Lactic acid, ethanol, carbon dioxide |
| 4 | The products change the food | Curd sets, dough rises, drinks fizz |
| 5 | Acid / alcohol also preserve the food | Low pH inhibits spoilage bacteria |

**Microbes in household food products — the master table**

| Product | Microbe used | What the microbe does |
|---|---|---|
| Curd / yoghurt | Lactobacillus (lactic acid bacteria) | Converts lactose to lactic acid; acid coagulates milk protein (casein); also increases vitamin B12 |
| Bread, dough | Saccharomyces cerevisiae (baker's yeast) | Ferments sugar to CO2; gas bubbles leaven the dough |
| Idli, dosa batter | Yeasts + lactic acid bacteria | Fermentation makes the batter rise and adds sour flavour |
| Swiss cheese | Propionibacterium shermanii | Produces CO2 holes and the characteristic flavour |
| Roquefort / blue cheese | Penicillium roqueforti (a fungus) | Grows through the cheese, ripens it with blue veins and sharp taste |
| Toddy (traditional drink) | Yeasts (natural fermentation) | Ferments sap of palm trees into an alcoholic drink |
| Dough for dosa kept overnight | Mixed natural flora | Souring + leavening in one step |

## 5. Worked examples and applications
≥ 6 worked examples with solved steps, live examples and Nepal-context applications (biology-plan.md §3.1, block V) — written in the unit fill pass.

## 6. Key terms and statements
Every new term defined once; exam-grade definitions live here and in keyPoints (block VI).

**Worked example.** Milk kept warm with a spoonful of curd sets in 4–6 hours, but the same milk left alone spoils instead. The difference is the **starter**: the inoculum gives lactic acid bacteria a huge head start, so they acidify the milk before spoilage organisms can take over. This is the whole logic of controlled fermentation — the right microbe, first and fast. It also explains why curd is safer than raw milk in places without refrigeration.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Five products with microbes — curd (Lactobacillus, lactic acid), dough/idli-dosa (bacteria + yeast CO2), toddy (Saccharomyces), cheese (Propionibacterium holes; Roquefort fungi), bread (Saccharomyces cerevisiae).
Trick 2: 'Roquefort cheese ripened by blue-green fungi; big holes in Swiss cheese from CO2 of Propionibacterium' — the two cheese specifics.
Trick 3: LAB converts milk to curd by producing lactic acid which coagulates casein and also checks disease-causing microbes — the dual benefit line.
